utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Today, on Tuesday, the 3rd of November, I would like to greet everyone present, the accused, the Defence teams, the expert witness, the Prosecution, and everyone else assisting us in our work. First of all, the Chamber would like to hand down an oral decision concerning the hearing of the witness Ivan Beneta that should take place from the 9th to the 12th of November 2009. The Chamber hereby decides to allocate three hours to the Petkovic Defence for their examination-in-chief and for any re-examination they might have. Given that there are no specific demands made by the other parties, the Chamber hereby decides to allocate an hour and a half to the other Defence teams and three hours to the Prosecution for the conduct of their cross-examination. The Registrar has informed me of how much time remains for the Prosecution. Madam West still has an hour and 41 minutes at her disposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam West, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours, Ms. Alaburic, everyone around the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Gorjanc. Yesterday, when we stopped, we were talking about P11081, which is a map, a BH map. There was some controversy arising yesterday regarding the scale of the map, but now you've had a chance to look at the map overnight. I also want to tell you that next to you, on your right, is the original map up here on the -- standing up straight. In addition, the map you have on the ELMO is a photocopy of the original map, so I want to ask you some questions about it. The photocopy you have in front of you, for purposes of the record, I have written on, and everyone has a copy of the one that I have marked. There is a blue line going up -- going vertically on the map, and that blue line follows the road. You'll see three dots, an A, B, and C. These dots are going to be the areas where I ask you to make an estimation of distance. And then there are also three numbers, 1, 2, and 3, that correspond with three pink areas on the map. So my first question for you, Mr. Gorjanc, is: Can you tell me what one block on this map, one square of this map, what that equals in distance?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, having carefully examined the map, I came to the conclusion that this is not a JNA map, a Yugoslav map. It's a NATO standards map, given that the scale is 1:100.000. That means that one square, one block, represents 1 times 1 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, if you look at the dot that is labelled A, do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. Mr. Praljak, only take the floor if you have a good cause. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do have a good reason to take the floor. In technical terms, this is erroneous. The scale of the map is 1:25.000, and everything is wrong. Judge Trechsel, we are mathematics. Our calculations are wrong. The scale is 1:25.000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You may think whatever you think, you may even be right, but you do not have the right to intervene here, to comment or criticise in any way what the witness says. So please sit down. That is the rule of these proceedings. Please sit down. You do not have this right, and we have to have some order in this courtroom. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Very well. Make sure that there is order. That we're discussing a map that is erroneous, it's a pity. We could proceed more expeditiously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, we started dealing with this issue yesterday, and General Praljak says that the scale of the map is 1:25.000, whereas you are claiming that the scale is 1:100.000. So we are facing a problem. You are both high-ranking officers, so one of you has to be wrong.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, on the original map on the screen, in the top left-hand corner it says quite clearly that the scale is 1:100.000; whereas, the map that was represented by using the ELMO is enlarged to such an extent that it is de facto a map the scale of which is 1:25.000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic. THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I really do apologise for intervening, but I have to draw your attention to the fact that there was probably a mistake when the scale of the map, 1:100.000, was placed on the map. If you'll have a look, you'll see that it says a map of Gorazde. It's not a map of Mostar. So someone stuck a part that wasn't really appropriate on the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Petkovic. What I told Mr. Praljak, of course, also applies to you. We'll see what the witness says. Your lawyers can ask questions when it is their turn, afterwards; but we do have to see to it that we keep the good order. And we'll see where we're getting. I think in -- on the fact, you're probably right, but we have to keep -- please, okay. THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, but I thought about this all night.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you say that it's a NATO map. Apparently, this map was drawn up for a situation on the 30th of June, to represent a situation on the 30th of June, 1993. I don't know who the author is, the ABiH, the HVO, someone from Mars. We really don't know. If it's the ABiH or the HVO, that means that at the time in 1993, you had access to NATO maps, at least those who compiled this did. But somewhat surprising, unless in the former Yugoslavia the Intelligence Service was so good that they were able to obtain NATO maps. That's possible by having recourse to spies. Could you explain why this NATO map was used by the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, first of all I would like to tell you that General Petkovic is quite right. On JNA military maps, the inscription -- the vertical inscription states the scale, and then you see the name "Gorazde." Usually, this was placed horizontally at the top of the map. How is it that it's now to the side and how is it that it says "Gorazde," well, I don't know. Secondly, I come to the conclusion -- or I came to the conclusion that it's a NATO map because there are certain markings that were not usually used by the JNA. That concerns the roads or routes that are marked in red throughout Bijelo Polje and Podvelezje. I assume that that's the case because those are the markings they used. However, the center of town and everything else resembles a JNA map, the scale of which is 1:25.000. Your Honours, when preparing my report, the Defence provided me with a map the scale of which was 1:25.000, at my own request, and today I prepared two maps so that we could clarify these matters. If you agree with this, I can provide you with these maps because I have electronic versions in PDF files.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll see about that, but perhaps the Prosecution will use your maps. Let the Prosecution proceed, and we'll see. Madam West, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do apologise. Could I just correct something in the transcript? On page 5, line 12, the witness said that you usually have a scale on JNA maps, and he mentioned an explanation, but there's something that is missing, because he mentioned the scale and the scale was 1:100.000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. West, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, for the purposes of the questions that I'm going to put to you in regard to this map, I want you to assume that the map to your right is the original map. I want you to assume that the map you have in front of you is a photocopy straight from the original map. Okay? Assume those for purposes of these questions. In addition, assume this map was created after the war. Now, I want you to look at the map on the ELMO, the map in front of you, at point A. Do you see point A?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Now, similar to what we did yesterday, using whatever formula you think is appropriate, I want you to tell me, between point A, going west to the HVO line, what is that distance?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's about 400 metres to the HVO line from point A over the bridge. I think the bridge is Tito's Bridge. So that's from point A to the HVO lines. It would be around 400 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Next to that A, can you write "400," please?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Now you see a B. Do you see the point B? From B, going west to the HVO front-line, what is your estimate of that distance?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The distance marked here is correct. It's 750 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And just next to the B, can you write "750" as well, just so we have that on the map?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Now, finally, do you see point C? This is in the area right below Rastani. We talked about that yesterday. From C to the closest border of Rastani, what is that distance?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If this is point C [indicates], this would be the shortest distance [marks], and it would be about a kilometre [marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: All right. So for the purposes of this question, I want you to assume for me that the HVO has taken over that area of Rastani where all those lines are, so that the edge of Rastani is the HVO front-line. Do you see that, the edge of Rastani near the point C? Tell me the distance between point C and the closest edge of Rastani.

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Towards the HVO lines, is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: No. What I mean is that point C close -- yes, from point C, I'm pointing at the dot, to the closest area of Rastani, which is this area right next to the dot, can you estimate for me how far that distance is?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's between 200 and 300 metres. However, Your Honours, this requires a minor explanation because the question arises as to whether the HVO forces were actually on the banks of the Neretva or were they in the depth at certain positions. I don't know where they were, but according to military principles, a river is defended from the depth, from appropriate positions. As to which positions would be appropriate here, well, the first appropriate position would be by the rail tracks, the embankment of the rail tracks, and the first houses of the Rastani settlement by the road and by the rail tracks, at the banks --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: I'm sorry for interrupting, but I would like to make this question more simple than that. I'm going to put a mark on the map with a red pen, so for the record, this is going to be my mark. And I want you to estimate the difference between point C and my mark.

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to be fussy again, but again it needs to be said what the mark is so that later people reading the transcript can see what it is. We can see it today, of course, but something like it's a short red line near to letter C, something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. West. Tell us that you are claiming that the red line is the HVO position when they took Rastani. Is that what you are saying? Is that what you are claiming?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Khan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I hesitate to rise. Of course, it's for the Bench to determine the utility of all of this questioning. For my part, I must admit that I've been somewhat at a loss. There is a scale, and rather than getting approximations in an imprecise manner, it seems to me that if this map is, in fact, accurate, the evidence that my learned friend wishes to adduce can be done in a far more scientific and accurate manner than the manner that's being given at the moment. Your Honour, there is a scale, and I'm sure these distances can be given from that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Khan, Mr. Khan, you are a very experienced lawyer, and you know better than anyone else that the Prosecution is trying to demonstrate, through this witness, that when the HVO was present in Rastani, at the banks of the Neretva, the road we can see -- where we can see point C was just a few metres away, in close contact. That's what she is trying to demonstrate. So the witness will answer the questions, and let's see how things develop.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, of course I will accept that, but I will note for the record that yesterday my learned friend put a great number of questions prefaced by the hypothesis, Assuming these facts to be correct, and then she put her question. It seems to me that having the benefit of the map, preparing for this cross-examination, aware that she was using this map, the more preferable -- the more accurate and more helpful way of proceeding would have been to, either through my learned friend's good offices or one of the many analysts the OTP have, calculate the relevant distances from the map and put it to the witness in the same form as yesterday. Assuming that point C to the line represents X distance, would you agree with that? But, Your Honours, at the moment I don't see how the Bench will be overly helped by the rather imprecise evidence that is being elicited from this witness, which does appears to be second rate compared to the scale of map that they are relying upon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's in the transcript now. Madam West, please continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would say that I fully agree with Mr. Khan. I think this proceeding is really losing a lot of time completely uselessly. I'm sorry. We have this map, and to have the witness estimate what everyone can, with a ruler that is scaled, find out for themselves, I see no point in it, frankly.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. West, put your questions to the witness directly. And I understand what you are trying to demonstrate, but put your questions to the witness, which will demonstrate everything you are attempting to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour, I am trying to do just that. So if I can continue. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, so the last point that we will talk about is C. I have put a red mark on the area, as indicated by the President that that is the edge of the Rastani HVO-controlled area. As the bird flies, just tell me the distance between point C and that red mark.

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between 100 and 150 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Write that on the map, please.

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may suggest something. I'm not objecting. [Interpretation] In regard to this question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I won't allow it. Let the Prosecution do its work. You're trying to prevent her from demonstrating her case. It's obvious, what she is trying to do. She wants to demonstrate that if the HVO was there, then point C was 100 metres away. That's all she is trying to show. Everyone can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I really want to make a contribution. There's just one sentence I want to say. I do agree with what you have said, but we have a problem with regard to determining the time-period. When did this happen? The map says the situation represents the situation -- the map represents the situation on the 30th of June, but we're assuming some other period is regarded. But I'm not asking for us to change the map and to have a map after the 30th of June, but in the question that is put, one should say that the situation was assumed, there's a hypothesis, it was a situation that one assumed was such after the 30th of June. That's all I'm trying to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. West, I didn't fail to notice the issue of the date, because on the 30th of June the map, with the HVO positions and the ABiH positions, was a certain kind, and then you say the HVO took Rastani. So tell us, when did this take place? That is what is missing. Mr. Kovacic intervened, but I was waiting for you to complete your questions to deal with the issue of the date. In your opinion, Ms. West, the HVO took Rastani and was on the banks of the Neretva when, exactly, on which date?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. This is something that we addressed yesterday, but just to remind everyone, I indicated yesterday and today that this map is subsequent to August 24th, 1993. And for the purposes of my questions, I included that in the assumption of facts for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, can you sign the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, Ms. West. So at the end of August 1993, in your opinion, the HVO was in Rastani, and you are claiming that they could have been on the banks of the Neretva at point C. Do we agree?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, can you sign your name at the bottom of this map and date it, please?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I have an IC number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll have a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The second marked version of document P11081 shall be given Exhibit IC1089. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, to clarify traveling on this road, during your direct testimony you had indicated that the route along the road, the main road that we're talking about here along the river, was easier at night; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: And why would that be the case?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I assume that at the time the equipment for nighttime observation was very expensive, it was difficult to obtain it, because all states that produced such equipment kept it in their own hands and it wasn't available on the black market. So the HVO probably did not have a sufficient number of devices for nighttime vision, especially not when it comes to using fire weapons, rifles, light machine-guns and machine-guns.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. Gorjanc, that's not my question. I asked you: Why would it be easier to travel that road, if you were travelling it and not an HVO combatant, if you were travelling that road at night, why was that easier? You testified to this during your direct testimony. Can you give us that answer, please?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Not a fighter of the HVO, but a fighter of the Army of BH.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: So is the reason that it was easier to travel that road if you were a civilian or a member of the ABiH during night, because there was less chance to be hit by artillery fire from the HVO than there would be during the day?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, the map and the road, we see very well that the road, after the 24th of August, could be under the fire of the HVO. That is a hypothesis. But a civilian or civilians, Muslim civilians, who wanted to leave East Mostar, looking at the map, there is the road, of course, and we all agree on that. But if they wanted to protect themselves, could they not go along the hill -- the bottom of the hill? There are hills of 400 metres, 700 metres. Wouldn't it be less risky for them to cross the hills in order to go to areas that were less exposed to HVO fire? Is this technically possible or was it possible? And I'm asking you this question because this morning I was looking at a photograph of Rastani, and we see Rastani and the river and then the hill, and the road, indeed, is exposed to HVO fire. That's clear. But there's the hill, and one could pass across the hill, yes or no, in military terms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there are two or three paths that they could have used, be it civilians or soldiers on foot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you say there are two or three paths that the civilians and soldiers could have taken. And if the Chamber were to go on site, we would take this path to check this. Unfortunately, when we went there, we didn't have all these problems in mind. Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, if you can go to list 2. It's the binder on the side. It will say "List 2." We're going to go to P04435, P04435. This is an August 23rd, 1993 SpaBat report, and in the English we're going to go to page 6. For the B/C/S, it's the area underneath the Jablanica-Konjic section. P04435. Do you see it? You probably have it on the screen in front of you by now. So in this document, SpaBat is reporting, and under "Jablanica-Konjic," it says: "Other information." "Officers of the HVO enclave told SpaBat that they would not allow any humanitarian aid convoys through on the road between Konjic and Jablanica unless the agreed exchange of prisoners between the HVO and the BH Army takes place on the 23rd, as planned." And then it says: "The convoy scheduled to proceed from Sarajevo to Jablanica has been delayed for 24 hours, so as to be able to provide security guarantees." The next paragraph says: "According to the BH Army in Jablanica, the Mostar-Jablanica road --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam West, the officer of the Chamber tells me that this document is confidential, so it shouldn't be shown. It is a document under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If we could go to private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, whilst members in court are searching for that document, may I say that we don't seem to be able to find it in the binder that's been provided by the Prosecution, and we would be immensely grateful for a copy of the same without delay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Just procedurally, Mr. President, my mistake. This is another document that should be in private session. I understand that this is in list 2. Is that not the case?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're now in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: P05692, P05692. This is a 7 October 1993 -- so this is about three weeks later -- document signed by Lasic, in which he -- it's entitled "Order for Defence." In the first paragraph, it says: "The Muslim Armed Forces within the 4th Corps ... in the general sector of the Mostar warfront, reinforced with 3.500 to 4.000 Muslim soldiers grouped in the area of Jablanica - village of Podgorani - the upper part of the village of Humi-Mostar, have the following task." And it lists the task, and the first is: "At all costs to have the Jablanica-Mostar route under control before winter." Assuming this is true, would you agree with me that this means that on October 7th, 1993, the Jablanica-Mostar route was not under the control of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Jablanica-Mostar road, following the Neretva River Valley, was not under the control of the ABiH in the sense, and I must note, it was not under the HVO control, but the HVO was able to act using artillery fire. But on the road, there were ABiH soldiers, so in actual fact it was under their control, but they couldn't pass because of the actions of the artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: You'll agree with me that anybody on that road, therefore, could not pass because of potential HVO artillery, therefore making the road impassable?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: I'd like to go to 2D1389. This is a document that you talked about on direct testimony, 2D1389, and it's dated July 1, 1993. And on direct testimony, you had indicated that you believed the 4th and the 6th Corps -- and the term you used or that you spoke about was "linked up," when you indicate -- when asked about "linked up," you indicated that meant unhindered communication. Could you please tell the Trial Chamber what exactly you mean by "unhindered communication"?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I meant under "unhindered communication" was passage across the western slopes of Prenj, across the villages and plateau of Glogova using mountain roads towards Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: So when you mentioned "unhindered communication," you were not talking about the main road; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Let's go to the end of the war. P08018, and this is going to be a document dated February 23rd, 1994. P08018. This the Peace Accord, and I'm going to specifically speak to the annex attached to it. So the exhibit, it's page 2 under number 1: "The following are to be accomplished in order of priority: "The opening of the following specified routes for humanitarian aid and UNPROFOR convoys, commercial traffic, and the passage of civilians, especially but not exclusively between: Zenica and Stari Vitez ..." And then the second road it mentions is Mostar-Jablanica-Konjic-Sarajevo. Sir, would you agree with me that this UN document indicates that at least by the end of the war, February 1994, the Mostar-Jablanica road was still closed to civilians?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise, but I really don't have the Croatian translation on the page. I see the English text, but it does not correspond to the Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: So you may go to your binder, sir, 8018, and the Croatian will be behind the English. Maybe the usher can assist.

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have found it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, the text in B/C/S is not the correct one.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So, Your Honour, to move things along -- and I'm not sure why e-court does not have the correct B/C/S, but if I may read it again slowly in English and have it translated for him for this document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, I'm going to read it again in English, and my apologies, I'm not quite sure why you don't have it. But this is the Peace Accord from February of 1994, and there's at the front page where there are signatures, but the second page is the annex to the Peace Accord. And number 1 of the annex says that: "The following are to be accomplished in order of priority:" And A, 1A, is: "The opening of the following specified routes for humanitarian aid and UNPROFOR convoys, commercial traffic, and the passage of civilians, especially but not exclusively between:" And it mentions four roads, and the first is Zenica to Stari Vitez. The second is Mostar to Jablanica to Konjic to Sarajevo. The third is Kiseljak to Vares. The fourth is Kiseljak to Bilalovac to Busovaca. So my question, sir, is at least in February of 1994, would you agree with me that the road from Mostar to Jablanica to Konjic to Sarajevo was still not open for the passage of civilians?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Now we've spoken at this point exclusively about the road going north. You also spoke in your direct about a road going south out of Mostar, and it was your testimony, and you tell me if you remember this, that there was some access to the south because you could see that they could go as far as Blagaj. And I want to show you 4D00622. This is a map created by the Petkovic Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. Witness, Madam Prosecutor has said, and you agreed with her, that the road did not allow for the passage of civilians, so you agree with her. That's fine. But what I would like to know is whether civilians could have passed using other roads and not just the route. That is what is important for the Judges. That is, the fact that there was artillery preventing the passage of civilians, was this a total obstacle or not for civilians and their passage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I based my claims on several documents which were issued by the Muslim authorities, and in doing so, I cited two documents from which we see that civilians were moving. One document says that soldiers, holding positions at Bijelo Polje, were not satisfied because civilians are moving unhindered towards the south. And in another document, which is actually a book by a Muslim author in which he says that columns would pass towards Jablanica and Mostar using mountain paths. And a third document, as far as I can remember, was a report of the Spanish Battalion -- the Command of the Spanish Battalion, which says that refugees from the area of Capljina were passing through Mostar, going to Jablanica. And I concluded from this that it was possible for civilians to use those mountain roads in the direction of the north.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam West.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may, a correction of the transcript. Page 22, line 22, the witness, referring to the first document, said that according to that document, civilians were able to go to the north and south of Mostar, whereas the transcript says only "south."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. In the French translation, there was mention of the south and north, and in line 22 it says only "south." But everything's fine now, it's been corrected.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could there be a correction in the e-court, because this document, 08018, doesn't have the translation in Croatian, but it has a different translation, and the Croatian translation does not correspond to the English text. So could we have the appropriate translation -- Croatian translation in the e-court for this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Madam Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, I want to talk about that south road that you had mentioned in your direct. And again 4D00622, this is a Petkovic Defence map, one that you've seen before. I think you probably have it directly in front of you right now; right? Now, on this map -- I understand that you did not draw this map, but that it shows the blue area, which is HVO-controlled area, and the green area, which is ABiH-controlled area. So for the purposes of this map -- I don't know if we can see it so well on e-court, but you have it in front of you. The bottom of your map extends off; correct? There's no cap of that green area?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: So let's show a map that's probably a little bit more fulsome. We'll go to 3D03724, 3D03724, map 11. This is a Praljak map of the same area, and it's the situation on areas under control of ABiH and HVO July 30th, 1993. Now, if you, sir, focus where -- do you have that map? My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This other one, 3D -- [In English] Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: So it's the loose bundle. There you go. So this is July 30th, 1993, and you'll see the area -- you can tell, from looking at this map, where Mostar is located; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: And if you look to the area towards the south, sort of where Blagaj would be located, that shows for you that that's where the ABiH-controlled territory ended; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: All right. So if you assume that that area stops there, you'll agree with me that beyond the area of Blagaj, which is included in the indictment as part of the sieged area under paragraph 110, that beyond the area of Blagaj the ABiH did not control anything south, Blagaj capped the area that they controlled; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: So let's finally move on to the mountain road that you have spoken about, and you've indicated a number of times that you believed the civilian population could go over that road. And on direct testimony, the document you cited in support of this was 4D719. And I would like to look at that document. I believe it's in the same binder. I'm sorry, it's in the loose one, probably right -- there you go. 4D719. This is a document you were shown by Ms. Alaburic, dated October 1993, and the part that she cited is on the second page of the English, so I'm going to read your testimony to remind you. She said, and she was quoting it, she said: "A large problem for the command of the operations group was presented by the transport of civilian population and everyone else marching north and south." And she said: "My question, Mr. Gorjanc, is: If you think back to that map that we looked at at the beginning of this examination, or, rather, as we first started discussing this subject, how would you explain this, the expansion of civilian population to the north and south?" And your answer was: "These people were probably moving down a mountain road and across the western slopes of Mount Prenj. The road must have been broad enough for them to be able to advance in both directions, north and south, without -- with no hindrance whatsoever." Sir, just to be clear, is this the only document upon which you base your opinion that the road was broad?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I never claimed that it was a broad road. I said that it was a horse path and that it could accommodate two columns of people on foot or horses, and that they could pass each other on that path.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Were you given any information about how far it was from Mostar to Jablanica over that road?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only conclude that based on the map, and I can say that it was anything between 20 and 25 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, it's true that you, yourself, have never been on that road; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's true, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: So I'd like to provide you with a different set of facts and see if your opinion remains the same. First, I want to share with you the testimony of Jeremy Bowen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. West, just a moment. To avoid wasting time, if I had known that you were going to insist, I would have given this a number. We had a witness who came and who was in Mostar -- and who arrived in Mostar after taking a road where there were horses through the mountain. I don't have the exact reference, but that witness did say that to us, and the Chamber heard that as a fact. We heard that from somebody under the oath who came to Mostar via a mountain road. I can't say whether that was a Prosecution witness. I think so. I don't have a reference, but maybe Ms. Alaburic can assist.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, several witnesses have spoken about that corridor, and I believe that at this point you are referring to the English journalist Jeremy Bowen who took that corridor several times and authored several stories, and he said that this corridor was known as the Ho Chi Minh line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's true. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: So I'd like to share with you some testimony and that is the testimony of Jeremy Bowen, and you're going to see it on the screen in front of you momentarily. This is from January 23rd, 2007. We're going to go through this slowly. The question was -- and I should say that Mr. Bowen was a journalist from the BBC and spent some time in Mostar. The question was: "Can you describe -- well, first of all, how long did it take you to then travel by foot from Jablanica to Mostar? "A. It took, I say, about 18 or 20 hours. It was a very long day and quite a bit of the night. We -- they had a caravan of about 20 or 25 pack horses, and I think some mules as well. Most of the horses and mules were carrying ammunition, and we rented from them four horse to put our equipment on, and we walked with the horses, and following the horses and following Humo, we walked 'til we got there. I mean, there was some delays in the route. We were shot at, at one point, and we had to wait there for -- until it got dark, until night fell and it was safe to go on." So let's stop there, and the first thing I want to talk about is this evidence that he was shot upon. Sir, would you agree with me that you had testified that there was no danger of being shot upon on the mountain road by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was random fire, because the HVO did not have any possibility to observe the road from Vrdi, where they had their mortar positions. I suppose that you're talking about mortar fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: And were you shown any documents to support that this could only have been random fire?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't been shown any documents. However, I can conclude that from my knowledge of fire, the way fire is opened from that kind of weapon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, a technical question, a military question. During the night, is there ammunition or materiel that can illuminate the area, and at that moment we will see in the sky an object which illuminates the entire area? At that time, did the BiH Army or the HVO have that kind of ammunition or materiel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suppose they did. I wouldn't know. But since the JNA had that, a certain number of flares, as they were called, that was part of everybody's -- every soldier's combat kit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And what is the surface that is illuminated by such ammunition, and from what distance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A mortar shell that is fired from a 120-millimetre mortar, at a distance of 3.000 to 4.000 metres, can illuminate a surface of 600 metres in diametre, and that illumination lasts for up to two minutes, approximately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: And so we'll just skip down to line 13, where Mr. Bowen was asked to talk about the footpath, and he said: "It was a single footpath, very steep in places. I was amazed the horses, some of which were very heavily laden, were able to keep their footing, and from Jablanica there was quite a steep climb up through wooded slopes, and then when you got to the top, there was a big mountainous plateau. There was a plateau surrounded by mountains, but open ground by then, and so a lot of the walk was through open ground. I mean, it was fantastic terrain. You know, it would be great to hike to do in peacetime, but over two days. We did it over a day; it was very tough." Mr. Gorjanc, this -- his memory of this route was that it was 18 to 20 hours, it was very steep, and it was a single path. Would you agree with me that this would not be the ideal escape route for children and elderly and the unfit to get out of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I couldn't agree that it took over 18 hours to pass that road. It is my deep conviction that during the night, even on horseback, it would be 2 to 3 kilometres an hour, which would make anything between 10 and 12 hours. The road is not favourable for the passage of children and women, especially if they carry something in their hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: And it's correct, sir, that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Prosecutor, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: It's correct, sir, that you, yourself, have never been on that path?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: I'd like to show you a video now on Sanction. It's P07431. This is a CNN report about East Mostar. Do you have the screen in front of you, sir? Can you see it? We'll play it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: "THE REPORTER: The Bosnian Muslims defending -- escaping the city of Mostar. This remote mountain track is the only strand of hope left for people driven by fear and desperation. Bedraggled, exhausted groups of men, women, and children haul themselves through more than 40 miles of physical endurance. It's a journey of sadness, an exodus of despair. Most of them are totally ill prepared for the ordeal. Many women walk over boulders in no more than slippers. The strong carry the weak. The old and hungry often collapse. They bring along just enough to survive, a little food, some water, a weapon to defend against robbers. Scattered, pitiful groups of people with nothing left, nowhere certain to go. "We found them many miles from their destination, after accompanying Bosnian government soldiers with pack horses. It was high in the Prenj mountains, another day's walk from journey's end, Jablanica far away. This was a place to rest, painful stories to tell. "SPEAKER: [Interpretation] We were expelled by the HVO Croats. Nine houses are burned and one mosque. They killed two of our men and set fire to their bodies."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: So, Mr. Gorjanc, I assume you've not seen this report before.

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not received interpretation, interpretation into Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. For the purposes of my question, it won't matter. I wanted you just to see the road. In regard to the stretch of the road that you saw, do you think, at least as far as this part of the road is concerned, it was not a broad road?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. Again, I'm not receiving an interpretation. I don't know why.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, are you receiving interpretation now?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Are you receiving interpretation now?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since this is already break time, we're going to take a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. West, you have 59 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, we're not going to go back to the video, because I didn't need you to hear what it was saying. I just wanted you to see what was on the screen. And would you agree with me that the mountain road that you saw on the video, at least that portion of it, was not broad?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that part of the road was not broad. However, it's not evident that that was, indeed, part of that road. I based my claim on the analysis of the map that was available to me, and on that map, that was a road that, in the one-time military we knew and we designated it as a horse path. And the average width of that was one to one and a half metres. It was more narrow at certain places and broader at others.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll go to P06365. This is the Jeremy Bowen video. I'm going to show you parts of this and ask questions. Do you see it in front of the screen? If you don't hear the Croatian, please tell me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: "THE REPORTER: Croatian propaganda echoing over the front-line in Mostar, the most vicious theatre of war in Bosnia-Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Did you hear the Croatian, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So in addition to physical factors in your report, in paragraph 205 you also wrote about psychological factors, and you listed them as combat operations, propaganda, and psychological operations aimed at the morale of the individual. Now, we started this video, and right before it stopped, what we heard was Croatian loud-speakers. Do you agree with me that propaganda is one of the elements you mention as part of the factors of a siege?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We'll continue for one more minute.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: "THE REPORTER: Since May, Bosnian Croats, aided and abetted by the Croatian government, have been laying siege to about 60.000 people in East Mostar. Almost all of them are Muslims, and they're fighting back hard. There are no safe places in East Mostar. You can be killed or maimed at any time on any street corner. Until it's happening, it's hard to realise how quickly lives can be destroyed. "Franjo Pavlovic, who was born a Croat, made the mistake of going out to repair some shell-damage on what had started out as a quiet morning."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, would you agree that shelling a civilian population might be also a factor in the psychological element you talked about in regard to a siege?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: We'll continue for a few more minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: "THE REPORTER: Life as a Muslim. The Croats expelled them over the front-line into East Mostar in August. He had one chance. A fire engine, the only one left on this side of Mostar, was nearby. Perhaps it could get him to the hospital in time. Nothing in her life before the war had prepared Mrs. Pavlovic for this. She's 53. After they married, she worked as an accountant in a graphic design business. The last traces of that life disappeared when her husband was hit. The streets were empty, and not just because of the shelling. There's a six-hour-long daytime curfew. The idea is to stop people getting hurt. "The hospital was only a few minutes away. Nothing is more than a few minutes away in East Mostar. The doctor hardly had to look at him. Mr. Pavlovic was dead. He'd been killed by shrapnel in the chest. For her sake, he went through the motions. He hadn't examined him yet, she said, Please do more. Everything, from the explosion to this, had taken about ten minutes. The hospital was ready for the next casualties. "SPEAKER: [Interpretation] This morning we were trying to repair our home. It was destroyed by a mortar. He stepped out to find out what the time was and to get some water so that I could wash our clothes. That's when it happened. "THE REPORTER: The more the doctors see, the more it hurts. They said they tried not to let it show. They'd been married for 32 years. The River Neretva cuts Mostar in two. These red buildings are on the east bank, the stronghold of the Muslim-led Bosnian government forces, but they have an important foothill on the otherwise Croat-controlled west bank as well. To get there, you have to cross the Old Bridge which was built in the 1500s. It's been hit many times, but it's still standing, just about. The Croats in the hill know that if the bridge falls, they will have savaged morale on the other side."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, you wrote that the psychological element is aimed at the morale of the individual. Would you agree that this bridge coming down in Mostar was a significant blow to the Muslim population of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not a blow just for the population of East Mostar. It was a blow for the entire humanity. It was a world heritage site. It was a cultural monument of global significance. And as such, of course, the destruction of the bridge did present a blow and affected the morale of the population in East Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: "THE REPORTER: A local cameraman called Miolan Smajlhodzic [phoen] documented the Croats' attempts to destroy it. He took these pictures. He's dead now, killed by a mortar a month or so ago. They were bringing bodies back from the front the day that we first crossed. The stretcher-bearers worked for a well-organised civil defence network. Men who aren't in the army have to take part. East Mostar, because it's so isolated, has become the Bosnian government's best-run and most highly-mobilised enclave. It has to be because they have so little. They had to hope that the blankets would hide them from the snipers. You can't move very fast when you're carrying a stretcher. Normally, they don't bother to bring the dead this far, but this man was alive when they started the journey and they wanted to try to get him to the hospital. They didn't see much point in turning back when he died."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, is sniping a form of the psychological element that you mention?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'm going to skip ahead in this video a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: "THE REPORTER: Most people only go out when they have to, once a day to the soup kitchen. Each container-full has to last a family 24 hours. There isn't much, but they all get about the same. The black market, which has corrupted Sarajevo, doesn't exist in East Mostar. Because hardly any aid gets into the city, there's nothing to buy or sell. It's all rationed."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Now, here it appears that there was no food because hardly any aid got in. Would you agree that the situation in Sarajevo was different in that respect because Sarajevo had more food?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour. I believe that we're asking from the witness to speculate. No factual basis has been laid for the question. It doesn't arise from the film that there wasn't any food. It does say that there wasn't much, but the quantities are not mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, your intervention doesn't serve anything. It just wastes time. You could have put that question in your redirect. Ms. West, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: "THE REPORTER: Civilians do as they're told. They have no choice. Organisation begins at the front-line. They have forward first aide stations. Nusreta Besic, who used to be a geologist, is in charge of this one. She runs it from her own home. She was treating one of her neighbours when there was another explosion. It was very close, even closer than they thought. Two men had been walking down the street. A lot of people live in this area. It's only a few hundred yards from the Croat positions. She slapped the man who was most seriously wounded to try to stop him going into shock. Passersby ran to help. Somebody shouted for some water. The man on the right died. They managed to save the other man. Not long afterwards, another emergency. A woman was lying on the riverbank. She'd been doing her family's washing. She was already dead, shot by a Croat sniper."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, here we have a sniping incident again, but my question for you is different. In accordance with your theory of All-People's Defence, that the entire population served the purposes of armed combat, then this woman on the bank of the river would have been a member of the armed forces; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the question is whether it was forbidden to go outside. She more or less went to the front-line to do her laundry. Well, that doesn't seem logical to me. No, she's not a member of the armed forces because she was doing her laundry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: What if she had been doing laundry for her son, who was a member of the ABiH? Would she then be considered a member of the armed forces because what she was doing was for the purposes of the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not even in that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Gorjanc, to be clear, it's your opinion that East Mostar was not under siege and that has much to do with the fact that it was not completely physically isolated. And I'll just remind you of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI HAD ASKED YOU
utterances.text: "In this light, would you agree, as a military expert, with the fact that one can say that Mostar is a city under siege, like Sarajevo, or that Mostar is in a different kind of situation?" And you said: "Mostar was in a substantially different situation." And the President asked: "How different?" You said: "To the north, where the main reserves of the BH army were, there were two roads leading. One was down the Neretva River Valley, which was most probably under fire, artillery HVO -- artillery fire. The other route took one across a mountainous area, the western slopes of Mount Prenj and on towards Jablanica. That route was not under fire by the HVO." So, Mr. Gorjanc, is it your testimony that physical isolation was foremost in your mind in making a determination that Mostar was not under siege?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: And it's also your opinion, then, that Sarajevo was under siege; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Because in paragraph 78 -- excuse me, 74, footnote 35, in your report, you wrote: "In besieged Sarajevo," and you bolded and underlined the "besieged Sarajevo," "some local commanders took civilians to dig trenches ..." The rest of the sentence doesn't have to do with the siege element, but I'd like to look at the physical factor when it comes to a siege. If we can go to P11067. It's list 2. I think you have it. P11067. This is a "Washington Post" article. I think there might be difficulty with e-court. Does everybody have this? I see the witness has it. It's in list 2.

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have it. I have it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: 11067. All right. I see that the witness has it, and I understand it's in list 2. So this is a "Washington Post" article, February 21st, 1994. The B/C/S parts that I'm going to read are translated, but for the English, it's paragraph 3, and it says: "'The 27.000 people crammed into Mostar's old city are living like rats,' said Jeremy Bowen, the chief UN relief official here. The city's inhabitants have had no clean water or electricity since the siege began. They've lived underground in cellars, storage areas, and basements day and night to avoid the constant shelling and sniper fire from Croat sharp-shooters across the Neretva River. Until last week, 60 to 70 shells exploded here on average." Skipping the next English paragraph, going to: "More people died here between May 9th, when the siege began, and mid-January than in Sarajevo, according to Alija Alkadic, a member of the local War Presidency, who keeps the figure on hand as a grim reminder. Alkadic has recorded 1.276 deaths here between May 9th and January 15th, compared to 1.097 in Sarajevo, which has a population estimated at nearly 400.000." I'm going to skip the next paragraph and then go to the following English one: "The Croat siege of eastern Mostar has made the Serb siege of Sarajevo positively porous. Here, there is no street market to buy even a loaf of bread or cigarettes, nor is there any kind of Serb-fed black market that flourishes in Sarajevo and helps keep people alive there, albeit at high prices in German marks." Mr. Gorjanc, this would indicate that the Mostar siege makes the Serb siege of Sarajevo look porous and that in Sarajevo you could buy bread and cigarettes, although it was a high price. If these factors -- or these facts were true, as compared to Sarajevo, would you -- would your opinion change that Mostar was not under siege?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wouldn't change, given that civilians were able to leave Mostar and go to free territory in the direction of Jablanica, whereas this was only possible in Sarajevo by using the tunnel, and it wasn't possible to reach a safe place. It was over the Igman Mountain. I don't know why civilians weren't able to leave Mostar. If I were a commander in the eastern part of Mostar, given the conditions in Mostar at the time, I would have attempted to get as many civilians as possible out of the town or to have a road or path built over the mountain so that it would be easier to bring in supplies.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to go to P11075. It should be in the same binder, P11075. And there's one English page, and it should be followed by a B/C/S page. And it's unclear to me whether you have -- you have a B/C/S there, but I'm not sure what the translation is. I'm going to read it in English, and I'll read it slowly in case the translation is not of this paragraph. It's page 326 of the English: "Most of the digging was done from the Butmir side," and we're talking about the tunnel in Sarajevo that you just mentioned, "(800 metres versus 120 metres from Dobrinja). The two tunnelling parties met underground on July 30th, 1993, in a triumph of engineering prowess and sustained determination. That same night, the army dispatched 600 soldiers from the besieged city to Mount Igman to reinforce the campaign to break the siege from the outside. The tunnel, called Object DB, resembled a kilometre-long horizontal mine shaft. Through it ran electric cables and a light rail system with wheelbarrow-like trolley cars. A constant inflow of groundwater required a pumping system to keep the tunnel from flooding. Passage through the tunnel was dark, damp, and demanding, and the tunnel averaged 1.7 metres in height, but one section was only a metres high, requiring a stooped and swift transit. For the rest of the war, the airport tunnel served as a conduit for arms, munitions, essential supplies and people." Mr. Gorjanc, I'm going to stop right there, and you would agree with me that for at least the people going through this tunnel, there was no risk of artillery fire; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: And the next passage is: "According to ABiH estimates, over a million person-passages were made through the tunnel from July 30, 1993, until the end of the war. British parliamentarian Paddy Ashdown, later the international community's High Representative for BiH, was among the few foreigners to traverse the tunnel. Bosnian President Izetbegovic travelled through it numerous times. Government officials of ministerial rank were accorded the courtesy of a trolley ride, although some of them declined and made the journey on foot, stooped over like everyone else. In addition to serving as a human passageway, the tunnel enabled the ABiH to transport weapons, ammunition, fuel, foodstuffs, and medical supplies. And according to its estimates, nearly 20 million tons of food passed through the tunnel into the city. This was less than the 31 million tons brought in under UN auspices by air, and it was dwarfed by the 168 tons delivered over-land in the UN-guarded truck convoys." Mr. Gorjanc, would you agree with me that assuming these facts about this tunnel are correct, that it would be much safer for a person to travel through this tunnel than for that person to leave Mostar by the main road under fire by HVO artillery or over the mountain donkey trail to Jablanica, that this tunnel was a much safer alternative?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The tunnel, itself, was safer, but entering the tunnel, leaving the tunnel, and going from the tunnel to the Igman slopes was dangerous. It was under Serb fire. However, the mountain trail over Glogovi [as interpreted] couldn't come under direct fire from HVO mortars because they didn't have such a range.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, if you apply the theory you applied to Mostar, that complete isolation -- complete physical isolation is a major component as to whether a siege took place, then you would also have to believe that Sarajevo was not under siege; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, only certain individuals in Sarajevo could leave the town, having obtained permission of the authorities. It wasn't possible for anyone to leave town when they wanted to. But given the documents I've seen, I could see that in Mostar, civilians could leave when they wanted to. I came to that conclusion because ABiH soldiers were uncomfortable because civilians could circulate freely.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, have you seen any document -- any HVO document, any ABiH document, suggesting that civilians could comfortably leave Mostar? When I say "comfortably leave," I mean safely leave, without risk to [sic] the HVO artillery fire on the main road or without risk of going over the mountain path from Jablanica. Have you seen any document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't seen any such documents, myself, but I did see one document. I can't remember what it was. It was a report on morale in a company in the area of Mostar, in the area of northern Mostar, and soldiers were uncomfortable because civilians could go in the direction of the north and the south. And also from SpaBat reports on refugees from Capljina, I could see there were refugees who would head off in the direction of Jablanica. I assume that they could go there unhindered by the Muslim authorities or, rather, by the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, in direct testimony last week, you spoke about the invaluable and inalienable rights of citizens to defend their country, and when you spoke about this in direct testimony, I believe you were quoting or you were talking about the SFRY Constitution. And the question from Ms. Alaburic was: "Article 237 of the document, it talks about how the defence of the country is an inviolable and inalienable right of nationalities working with people and citizens. Let's look at citizens for the time being," she said. "Given your military expertise and your familiarity with these regulations, what does this mean, inviolable and inalienable right in terms of defence?" And you said that: "That means that no one can deny anyone else the right to put up resistance, to resist." You further said that: "No later regulation contradicting the Constitution could be applied in this sense, in the sense of preventing someone from putting up resistance." Mr. Gorjanc, would you agree with me that the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and this would include the Muslims, had the same right, and that would be they had the same right to join up with the ABiH and defend their rightful territory against any occupying force, according to the Constitution you quoted?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what the Constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina also states, in the same terms as the Constitution of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to show you a map, P09276. You looked at this with me early on in the -- your testimony. Can we have Sanction for the witness, please. Do you see that map in front of you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: You remember -- thank you. You remember seeing this last week; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: And your testimony last week was that this territory outlined in red, beginning in December of 1990, after the elections, until at least the middle of 1994, remained the sovereign territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: And does it then not follow, sir -- strike that. Let me back up a minute to show you -- or read to you some of your direct testimony, and this is from last Tuesday, from Ms. Alaburic. She said: "Mr. Gorjanc, we shall now move on to the doctrine of All-People's Defence. But before that, we will also be talking about laws regulating the Yugoslav People's Army." And she said: "But let's clarify your answer as to -- the Yugoslavs' People's Army at one point became an aggressor in any of the territories of the former Yugoslavia. If I understood you correctly," the question she asks is, "you said that the Yugoslavs' People's Army could not have been an aggressor in the territory of Yugoslavia for as long as Yugoslavia existed; is that correct?" And your answer to her -- to counsel was: "Yes." So, Mr. Gorjanc, my question to you is: Does it not then follow, in looking at this map, that the ABiH could not be considered the aggressor on any of its own territory, as outlined by the red line?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I ever claimed that the ABiH was the aggressor in Bosnia or anywhere else in the territory of the former state.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: So is it your testimony that the ABiH was never an aggressor, in 1992 and 1993, in the war between the ABiH and the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to object to the imprecision of the question. An aggressor in relation to Bosnia and Herzegovina or in relation to some other entity?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: The term "aggressor" I'm using comes directly from Ms. Alaburic's question, so let's -- let's ask it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Is it your testimony that the ABiH was never an aggressor, in 1992 and in 1993, in the war between the ABiH and the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In formal legal terms, it wasn't the aggressor on its own territory. Bearing in mind the fact that the Croats and the Serbs had the very same right, to defend their territory, the question then arises as to who the aggressor was in that unfortunate war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, so that it is very difficult to determine who the aggressor was. International experts or, rather, experts in international law would find that very difficult, and let alone myself, as a member of the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: So, Mr. Gorjanc, let me just go to your answer, where you said: "Bearing in mind the fact that the Croats and the Serbs had the very same right to defend their territory ..." And I'll stop there. If we can go back to Sanction, back to that map that we spoke about earlier. You'll agree with me that the area within that red line is not Serb territory and it is not HVO territory, that is sovereign BH territory; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the sovereign territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but it's not Muslim territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gorjanc. That was not my question.

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how it should be put.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: And that was not my question, but the next question is: Following that, then, during the HVO-ABiH war, the HVO was the aggressor on that territory within the red outline; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The HVO couldn't be the aggressor in its own territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Can you show me, sir, on the map in front of you, within that red line, what territory was the sovereign, independently -- independent, internationally-recognised territory of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, now I really have a serious objection to this question, because this question implies that the HVO wasn't an armed force that was also defending Bosnia and Herzegovina from a common enemy at the time. So I would, therefore, ask my learned friend to first determine the territory of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina so that we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The objection is dismissed. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Your answer was: "The HVO couldn't be the aggressor in its own territory." Now, you have the map in front of you, and my question is: On that map, within that area of the red line, what territory was the sovereign, independent, internationally-recognised territory of the HVO? Is there any area within that red line that is the sovereign territory of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to international law, well, not a single part of the territory was recognised that was under the jurisdiction of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: So, Mr. Gorjanc, then as -- if I -- let me ask you this next question. If not a single part of the territory was recognised that was under the jurisdiction of the HVO, then is the answer to my question that there is no HVO territory in that red line, no HVO sovereign territory? Is that the answer to my question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, why are you on your feet again? Because the Judges fail to understand?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours. I'm certain that you understand everything. But one day another Chamber will have to consult this transcript, and I believe that I have to state that after the first sentence, the witness wanted to continue, but he was interrupted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, were you interrupted, or was your answer cut off or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there was something else I wanted to add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid that one is trying to identify Bosnia and Herzegovina with the Muslim state. This was an internationally-recognised state that was composed of all the ethnic groups that lived there, the Serbs, the Croats, and the Muslims. It's not for me to assess why a conflict broke out between these three peoples. Being familiar with the history of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I could say that such things occurred in that area every 30 or 40 years, and I cannot claim that one people defending its territory was at the same time the aggressor in relation to one of the other peoples that also laid claim to a certain part of the territory. Bosnia was an entity that was composed of three constituent peoples. That's what was stated in the Constitution of the SFRY and of Bosnia and Herzegovina. As far as I know, that is contained in the Constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina as well, the Constitution that was drafted in 1992. And, therefore, I draw the conclusion that not a single people could be said to have been the aggressor in that state. All the other units that arrived from the outside and hadn't been called in had no justification to be there, or if they had no justification to be there, they were the aggressor, and that also includes the remainders of the former JNA that was withdrawing from Slovenia and Croatia to the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, last Wednesday -- I'm going to read to you a question that counsel put to you, and your answer. And Ms. Alaburic said: "Mr. Gorjanc, let us posit this security threat and let's say it actually happened." And she went on to say: "You're an HVO commander, losing control over a significant portion of your own territory simply because you were betrayed by soldiers of another ethnicity from within your own ranks. What sort of reaction would you have put in?" And your answer was: "I would have considered that to be an act of treason, and I would have taken any steps available to me, including the pressing of charges against those deserters." So, sir, I want to ask you a similar question, but I'm going to change the facts a little bit. My question is: You were an HVO commander, losing control over a significant portion of territory that was not yours. It belonged to Bosnia-Herzegovina, an independent, internationally-recognised sovereign state. And the reason you lost control was because soldiers from within your ranks used their inalienable right to support the ABiH and resist the occupation of the HVO. Sir, would you -- what I just -- the hypothesis that I just read out to you, would you have considered that to be treason against the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would continue to consider this to be treason, since those soldiers were within the ranks of the HVO military and fought with the Croats against the Serbs or, rather, the remnants of the JNA in the territory of Mostar. And once they abandoned that and captured Croatian territory, then they were traitors.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, isn't treason a crime where the victim is the state, a crime that is directed against a state?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a purely legal category, and I'm unable to comment on it. You are certainly more familiar than myself. For me, treason is if somebody turns around against me; he was with me until yesterday, and suddenly he turns against me. For me, that is treason.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEST
utterances.text: I want you to assume that the definition of "treason" is: A violation by a subject of his allegiance to his sovereign or to his state. I want you to assume that to be true. If any of these soldiers betrayed the HVO, Mr. Gorjanc, it could not be an act of treason, right, unless Herceg-Bosna was holding itself out as a state; that's correct, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was betrayal, treason, regardless of whether the HVO was considered to have its own state or not.
