These men abandoned the common front-line ranks and turned against what used to be their co-fighters, regardless what lofty goals they had in mind. I point out Bosnia and Herzegovina was not a state of Muslims. It was a common state -- a joint state of all three constituent peoples and other peoples living there.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gorjanc. Mr. President, I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Concerning re-examination, Madam Alaburic, you have five minutes. As you asked for four hours, the decision of the Chamber was four hours for the examination-in-chief, including re-examination. So what is your position now?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we asked for four hours for the examination-in-chief, and at the time of submitting our request, we were unable to assess whether we would need any re-examination, and if we would, for how long. At that point in time, we could not also assume --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Alaburic, I stop you. The guide-lines of the Chamber were very clear, and they have been applied to Mr. Karnavas. When we fix a duration for the testimony of a Defence witness, within that time-period there is the examination-in-chief and the re-examination. That is a guide-line. Therefore, don't try and change our guide-lines. You may, perhaps, have questions to put. You must tell us on which points and make an explicit reference to questions put by the Prosecution, because as the Rules say, the re-examination has to be directly linked to examination-in-chief. You cannot embark upon another issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely so, Your Honour. We had no intention, in the redirect, to embark upon any new issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How much time do you need?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak would also have a few questions linked to military issues, and in view of the fact that we had this map and both generals have a large number of observations to make, and I would like this to go into the transcript, General Praljak has prepared a redirect that would last about one hour. Since you gave the Prosecution six times more time than we had to re-examine their military expert --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Alaburic, it is absolutely out of the question for General Praljak to take one hour. When a witness comes, we assess the time for the examination-in-chief, the re-examination, and 50 per cent of the time we give. The others had two hours for this, and you have to be very careful about this. My question to you is, because this is your witness: How much time do you need for the redirect?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is a joint witness for the Defence of General Praljak and General Petkovic, so I think you should grant us this request. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] About 20 minutes, 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And me, I assume a little longer than half an hour. That would be quite sufficient. I believe that those questions would be important. If you consider something to be unimportant, I will stop the questions. And in that case, I think we could complete this testimony today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For General Praljak, 20 minutes, and you need about 40, 45 minutes; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak said he needs 25 minutes, so let us agree that we can complete this matter by 7.00 this evening. I will confer with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber rules that all the time that is going to be used now shall be detracted from your credit, of course. Secondly, we will stop at 7.00 p.m. with the re-examination. Therefore, try and be -- to be precise, to avoid objections, because that causes a loss of time. When you have questions, you will say, Madam Prosecutor asked you such and such, and then you put your question. Do we agree now? And you must say what topic you're going to discuss; the siege of Mostar, the civilians, or I don't know what else.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm very grateful for this decision. And according to our internal decision, we would like General Praljak to start with the re-examination, and I will take over later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, do not forget to tell us what you are going to put your questions about and to refer to the questions already put. As I know you take notes, it will be easier for you to do this. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Everything will be in accordance with the Rules of Service, as we say in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Gorjanc. The topic is: Was Mostar besieged by the HVO. I don't know about the Serbs. Do you know what the relationship between the ABiH and the Army of Republika Srpska, in 1993, in the surroundings of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no documents about this, but on the web I found a large number of documents or reports according to which representatives of the BH Army traded with the Serbs in the territory around Velez. I'm not saying for certain, but that meeting was attended, in addition to Arif Pasalic, by even General Mladic, a Serb general, for a certain period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you please -- I want the document 4D00719, 4D00719. It is a document dated the 14th of October, 1993. You have it on the screen now. It is the 4th Corps Command, signed by Chief of Staff Mr. Esad Ramic. Do you see the document, Mr. Gorjanc?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Look, please, on page 1. We'll skip over the part referring to prisoners, but towards the end of the first page you will find the words, I quote: "In addition to this, it has been established that it is necessary to stop the traffic along the main road while relieving personnel at positions held by this company." And then it goes on to say: "Due to the more difficult manoeuvre towards the town, it is necessary to cut down trees and clear the way across Kandiljan." My question: What does this mean, that it is necessary to stop the traffic when the troops are taking over their duty? Does this mean that there was traffic along that road, and it was so intensive that it is in the way of the troops when they're taking over their duties?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object to the form of the question, beginning with: "Does this mean ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, do not put leading questions. Put your questions in an open-ended way. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: What does this mean, to stop the traffic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means that the traffic was so heavy that it is in the way of the troops going to take over their duty. Let me explain what "across Kandiljan" means.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: No, we'll come to that. On page 2, it says that: "The deputy corps commander, Sulejman Budakovic, Tetak, six days ago," which means on the 8th of October, "ordered to stage assault against the dam area by using all available weaponry in order to disencumber our units," that is, units of the ABiH, "operating towards Vrdi." My question: Do you know when the Neretva-93 offensive started, how long it lasted, and along which axis?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not study that operation because not in context, but I know that it was in September 1993 and that activities were directed towards Prozor and Trnica [phoen]-Vrdi.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Page 3, I quote: "A major problem for the command of the operations group is the transport of the civilian population and others marching in the direction of the north and the south. That is why it is necessary for the civilian authorities to take over control of civilian transport." Could you comment on this? How is this transport carried out, and where are those people going?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I have already spoken about this in my testimony. I referred to this document several times. This refers to the road across -- along the slopes of Prenj Mountain that the English journalist referred to as the Ho Chi Minh Trail.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Gorjanc, in answer to a question by the Prosecutor, you agreed with certain positions emanating from a certain text. My question is: Did you, yourself, use those road along -- around Mostar, Tepcici, Bijelo Polje, and so on?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, several times, because I was frequently in Herzegovina. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Now we move on to the maps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. I do not wish to waste time, but I discover this sentence from the October -- from the 4th Corps. I assume that what is written corresponds to the reality. One has the impression that the army does not want to concern itself with this issue of transport, and they wish the civilian authorities to take over. But in their writing this, then it means that there are people passing there; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is obvious from the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Witness, I seem to detect certain inconsistencies. Here, they speak of transport of civilians. What do you understand under the term "transport of civilians"? What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think the author of this document had in mind the passage of civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Is the translation wrong? I don't want you to interpret and suppose what the author thought. I ask you: What does "transport of civilians" mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The transport of civilians would actually mean transporting civilians in vehicles or on horseback.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Right. That's how I would also understand it. Now, you said that that was a transport over the Ho Chi Minh path. That is the one we have seen experts of individual; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You will not say that you think that vehicles transported civilians over that path? Do you say that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I never said that anywhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Okay. Then something here is unclear. Plus another point. Mr. Praljak asked you, Have you been on these roads? And you have answered, Yes. And these roads, in the context, must include the path on which previously you told us two or three times you have never been. How do you solve this, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, on this particular path, I never was, but I would frequently travel Sarajevo-Jablanica- Mostar along the main road, and I frequently stayed, in the former times, 30 years ago, in the area of Dubrava, because the father of my late wife was born in Dubrava.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: That is not contested, but we were talking about the passage in the text which you said referred to the mountain path, and Praljak asked you, Have you been on all these mountain roads? And it would have been honest if you had said, On most of them, but not on the Ho Chi Minh path, because you have created certain doubts. Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you are quite right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. Witness, I did not refer to this question of passage along the Ho Chi Minh path, but one needs to read the whole sentence, but if I make a mistake, don't hesitate to correct me. My impression is that the author of this document is raising an issue linked to the transport of civilians, and specifically to wounded civilians, because wounded civilians would, a priori, not be transported on horseback. And he says, in continuation of this stage -- of this sentence, that it is necessary to repair the armoured vehicles and adjust it for this purpose, and during the night, because there might be fire. So my impression is, then, that reading this document, there is the transport of civilians that can be done on board vehicles, specifically wounded civilians, and then there's another category of civilians who are not wounded, who are walking towards the north and toward the south. According to you, in military terms, is that the description given here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the description is correct, but I think transport by armoured vehicles refers to wounded people in Bijelo Polje, Salikovci [phoen], Potaci [phoen], in the direction of the hospitals -- to the hospital in Mostar, and not wounded civilians towards the north, towards Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. General Praljak, I apologise for intervening, but I think that the sentence required some clarification. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] I'm very pleased, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Just once again, we're talking about Ho Chi Minh that Bowen refers to, but you were not there and no one has been there. We're talking about the document. What does it mean, to stop the traffic? Is this movement of people or movement of vehicles?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is movement of vehicles, and this refers to point C that Madam Prosecutor marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Is it possible to conclude from this that vehicles were moving in such numbers that they're an obstacle to the ABiH when soldiers are going to take up their shifts? Please look at this map first. Madam Prosecutor told you that this map was prepared by the Bosnia-Herzegovina authorities. Is it correct that the scale is incorrect?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: How many brigades are shown on this map as belonging to the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three brigades, the 41st, the 47th, and the 48th.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Were there any other units, outside those brigades in the documents, which altogether constituted the 4th Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was the 42nd Brigade, and I have no information as to its location, but its territory was the broader area of Pijesak -- Pjesci. I don't know whether this was true for that particular point in time. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Mr. Gorjanc --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could we note in the transcript we're talking about 11081, map number 11081. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: You have elements of siege which this body of Bosnia-Herzegovina drafted and stated, and we don't know who signed it, and he described Mostar as a concentration camp. How can four brigades be situated in a concentration camp? Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: It says here that supply of power, electricity, water, and gas was stopped. Did you ever hear Mostar having any gas?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Maybe bottled gas, butane gas.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: I'll now give you a map where certain mortar positions have been marked, and of tanks, of the HVO, so please have a look. And here's another one. Will you take it, please? Will you look at the more -- range of mortars, assuming they're 82 and 122 millimetres, can they reach all the areas of Bijelo Polje, Vrapcici, and the rest?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Please put the second map on the ELMO. Will you please mark that map with your date and signature?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: My question is: This map of the 30th of June, 1993, do you know who had control over the Bjela Bridge, until when?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. However, the road that goes via Glogova towards Jablanica went along the Bjela Valley, which means that the bridge was destroyed but there was a roundabout way.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know or did you see a document showing when the second lane of the Bjela Bridge was destroyed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know until what date the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina controlled Rastani or was in Rastani?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree with me that when it comes to military maps, every time every change should be marked by a date?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Look at the following map. Could you please put the map on the ELMO? This is a map of Mostar. Could you please show it to all of us? Take a pen and show us how many parallel streets in the city of Mostar there are from north to south. The Prosecution showed you just one street.

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Four, and in some places there are as many five.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes, four, you're right. Very well. And now could you please tell us -- can you take a pen and show us at least two or three parallel streets from north to south, and can you mark the map with your signature and date?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main one through the city [indicates], the bypass along the mountain slopes, and there is another one from the Old Bridge up to the Carinski Bridge and then connects with the Main Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Could you please mark them with 1, 2, 3?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: And then another one that goes between the bypass and the Main Street which was once known as Marshal Tito Street. Put 1, 2, 3, 4 next to them.

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks] THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Can the witness have a better pen? Mine is red. It's better. We won't be able to see a thing on the map otherwise. And your signature, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's give an IC number to the map. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] And the previous one as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, just this one.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the map just marked by the witness shall be given Exhibit IC1090. Thank you, Your Honours. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] One more question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, do you know that from the railway station in Mostar, across the entire city of Mostar, there is a railway tunnel?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Which means that you can use that tunnel and pass through Mostar, sheltered from everything and everybody; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Objection. Mr. President, objection to the form again. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Very well. Can we please have the following map?

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: And, Mr. Gorjanc, this is a map whose scale is 1:25.000, just like the one that was shown to you by Madam Prosecutor, and it demonstrates precisely what we have forgotten. And I'm talking about Kandiljan.

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kandiljan.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: You're going to show us, on this map, how behind Gradina, across Kandiljan, where you can go and what you can reach, and you're going to mark all that for us. The document number, 4D00719, says that it is necessary to cut the branches on the road towards Kandiljan. Mr. Gorjanc, could you please show us that road?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation] [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to correct the record. Line 11, page 44, the general is talking about a map whose scale is 1:25.000, which you can see in the map. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, is number 2 here the area of Kandiljan?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: And what about number 1; is that the hill called "Gradina"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A problem. There was a mistake in the transcript. You did say "20.000," Mr. Praljak, but it is 25.000, is it not? Ms. West -- THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Correction, I said "25.000." Your Honour, I could not make that mistake, because there is no 20.000 scale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, this witness was purported to be an expert on military general subject matters. He is now testifying on factual matters in Mostar. I was very careful, when we put the map in front of him, to assume certain facts. The reason that this becomes important is if later the Praljak Defence looks to admit these maps, you now have an expert, who's never been purported to be a factual witness, trying to authenticate maps, so I object to any factual evidence coming from him, and I put the Praljak Defence on notice: I would object to the admissibility to any of these maps.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, while we're sorting things out, I do wonder, perhaps it's my misunderstanding, but when Mr. Praljak suggested that the first of those two maps he'd shown the witness, in quick succession, should also have a number. Your Honour said, No, just this one. But if that one doesn't have a number, we've got a document which is different from any other map in the case which was referred to in the course of examination, and, therefore, in accordance with normal practice, it would need a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: There's an error, Mr. Stewart. We have always refused giving numbers to maps that were not in any way marked by the witness. They can be directly put on IC and have an admission, like any other document, only when the witness marks the map. Then he signs, then we give a number IC. That's the way it's always been.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, [overlapping speakers] my confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You are excused.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, he signed it. Mr. Praljak, having added some marking which the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: He should not have.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- then alluded to. Well, Your Honour, I'm lost as to what happens to it, but Your Honour is the judge and I'm not, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. West, to answer your objection, you said that he was not a fact witness, which we agree with. The first map to which we have given an IC number, the witness showed us that there were four streets. He marked them with numbers 1 to 4. So whoever did it, you or somebody else, he marked them. And the second map that we see now, General Praljak is asking him to pin-point an area, and this is what he has just done. Nobody -- anybody else could have done that. For me, you don't have to be an expert or a fact witness to do that. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I don't, Your Honour, because the difference is the first map he showed him, he was just marking roads that were going north and south. The question on this most recent map that Mr. Praljak has is line 16 at page 64: "You're going to show us on this map how behind Gradina, across the Kandiljan, where you can go and what you can reach, and you're going to mark all of that for us." That's quite different. He has to have some factual understanding of this to know, You go down this street you take left, you take a right. That is a very different answer to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, just a slight detail. If my dear colleague [overlapping speakers] would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: -- would know the locations, then would see that it is the same question. It is exactly what she was asking, the only difference being that General Praljak - and obviously the expert - are aware of particular locations, what is the name. That is the only difference. It is the same set of questioning, the same subject matter. And by the way, the expert just mentioned, before General Praljak asked, one of those locations, Kandiljan. He mentioned it, without being asked about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, sir, you said that you were in Mostar. The area of Gradina, is it an area that you're familiar with? Have you been there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was never there, not in that part; however, I'm familiar with that area. Yesterday, you provided me with a map. I did that, and I memorised those places because already yesterday the Prosecutor asked me about that place, and that's why I studied that place in detail, and I studied it based on the map that you provided to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Colonel Gorjanc, if there is that road, indeed, behind Gradina Hill, across the area that is mentioned in this document that I have just cited, would the traffic through that area, owing to the protection given by the hill and the houses, would that traffic be complete and protected from the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't agree completely. It is not protected from mortar fire. It is protected from infantry fire and artillery fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: However, bearing in mind the distance for mortars of 120 millimetres, that would be the ultimate range, and 80-millimetre mortars can't reach this, bearing in mind the drawing or, rather, the sign depicting "mortar."

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Very well. One more question. According to your familiarity with the confederation, could one from any point --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. I have a preliminary question. On this map, Witness, you have drawn a red line across, underlining practically the word "Kandiljan," whatever that means. On the map, I cannot find any road at all that leads from the bottom of the hill somehow back to the street. Can you comment on this? Perhaps I am inept, but I see no -- I see the word "Kandiljan," but that's not where you can transport.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, no, you can't transport. This is a path for people on foot and, exceptionally, cattle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to read the last sentence from the document 4D00719: "Due to an impediment over towards the city, the branches on the road over -- leading to Kandiljan have to be cut." This is from the document of the BiH Army. We don't know how wide this road is, but it does connect certain houses and buildings. What does it mean, this term "broncage" or cutting branches?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This means to clear up the area of the road and around the road because that area was mostly covered by shrubbery, by the very low Mediterranean shrubbery.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Okay. We will not go over that any longer. Can we have the following map, which is 1:50.000 and shows the northern part of Mostar, Mostar and its northern part? Could we please have that on the ELMO? Could you please sign the previous map, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, can we give a number? If it doesn't have a number, we have to give this a number, this map that depicts Kandiljan.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The most recent map just marked by the witness shall be given Exhibit IC1091. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your leave, could I have the map back to sign it? I forgot to sign it. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You don't have to, because in the transcript it's very clear. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, the first map that I showed you, which was a copy of the Prosecution map where I marked the range of mortars, you confirmed -- or, rather, did you confirm that that was correct? If that was correct, could you please sign that map? And can I ask to have an IC number for that map?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I have the map back?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first map that we saw, the Chamber does not accept that map. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] And the last map, could the witness be provided with the last map, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It would be helpful if you gave the number of the map, because otherwise the record does not know which is the next one. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] 3D00850 is the map we already saw, but to a different end. 3D00850 is a military map of Mostar to -- the scale is 1:50.000.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, General. What I have now is a map of 1:25.000. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] You have to sign that one. We have already finished with that map. All it takes for you is to sign it, and then I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, you have confused us now with all the maps. We have given two IC numbers. That should suffice. And now you are going to show the witness a new map. That's the way I understood you. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is the rest of the area towards the north to show how many roads -- how many paths there are in the villages north of Mostar. There are 30 different possibilities, but let me not speak on behalf of the witness. This is the map. Let the witness talk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Usher, could you please provide the witness with that map, with the new map. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] We have it here. Could you please move to the northern part on the map? But it's better to put it on the ELMO, because we will then be able to see it in its entirety in colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: The northern part, Colonel, sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, in the meantime let me tell you the following: You were given 20 minutes, and let me qualify that -- clarify, rather, that although it was mentioned that those 20 minutes should be taken away from the Defence 2D, but, on the other hand, you have still, in a way, timing which you can also use for yourselves, and that is why I believe that your time will be accounted on your Defence, that is, Defence 3, it is my first point. My second point is that you have been given, as I just mentioned, 20 minutes. I would like to ask the Registry how many minutes have you used so far. I believe it is much more than 20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Twenty-three. So I was now told that you used 23 minutes, so kindly try to finish with your questions, if possible, within a few minutes now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise. On line 22, page 71, it says in the transcript that Mr. Praljak will be using the time of 2D Defence. We don't mind, but that was not the spirit of the Chamber's decision. That's why I stood up to intervene.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's usually the Presiding Judge who should announce this. Mr. Praljak, the time that you spent, 23 minutes, plus the following minutes will be deducted from your three hours, so -- I forgot that you had three hours. You used 23 minutes, which will be deducted from your three hours, and that doesn't apply to Mr. Petkovic's Defence. As Judge Prandler said, could you please bring your questioning to an end, after having shown that last map to the witness. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Yes, I will bring my questioning to an end. This is my time and Ms. Alaburic's time, and I don't think that in situations where it takes five minutes to bring the map to the witness -- it's impossible. Maybe I should better sit down and maybe we should accept the most unbelievable thesis of Ms. Prosecutor that there was just one road.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Colonel, could you please take a pen, and can you please show us several ways how one could get from Mostar behind -- you will see here -- could you please blow up? You have and I've given you the magnifier. Look at the exit from Mostar behind Gradina, Kandiljan. Yes, stop. Good. Excellent. Could you please start drawing, starting from number 2? Can you start drawing routes? So number 1, that's the highway. Of course, you're right. What about where you see number 2, can start drawing from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I think that a better pen should [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, could you please put the figures in squares? There are already circles, and as you are drawing routes, could you please put numbers in squares? Otherwise, we're going to mix things up. Mr. Stewart reminded us yesterday that we have to be very precise.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks] THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Could you please connect Gradina with Kandiljan, behind Gradina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: And could you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: We have just seen that this is not a road. This is a footpath for a person walking or a cattle. Mr. Praljak, please do not confuse things. We have had this on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness is being confused by the way it was put. He was asked to put numbers in squares --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry. There was a reference to numbers already in circles. He was asked to put numbers in squares. I don't think he quite appreciated that it was a new set of numbers. It could be that letters might be better. Although, just a tiny suggestion, but that's what happened. So the square around number 2 is just a complete mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Sir, when I said that you should put the numbers in squares, I was referring to your numbers, but you have put squares around the numbers that were already there. Use letters, A, B, C, D, and then indicate the paths that could be roads or that could be footpaths.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel for Mr. Praljak -- microphone for Mr. Praljak, please. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Towards the north. Have a look at the paths to the right and mark all the paths that lead up to number 6, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: These are roads, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: How far are they? How far are these roads from HVO positions?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends. Given that in the area of Potok, the HVO was on the left bank, so in some cases it's 500 metres away, but on average over a thousand metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Have a look. From number 7, Jasenjani, is it possible to go to Bjela by route, and is this a route that could also be used by cars?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, on the basis of the map I had at my disposal, the road in question is a dirt road that could be used by vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. This map has a scale of 1:50.000. Have a look here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, the Chamber believes that we have understood that there are roads -- routes that make it possible to go from Mostar in the direction of the north, northwards. This is something that has been confirmed by the witness. He's marked certain locations, A, B, C, D, so now you can just say, Well, these routes, these paths, and this is what you want to demonstrate, in fact. And in addition, you have also used up all your time, so we have to conclude now. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] I will, Your Honours, I will conclude, but one more question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: In the document, I quote: "Order the Civilian Protection to repair and cut off the road through Kandiljan," or clear up the road. Sir, how old were these military maps when this was written, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, I don't agree with Judge Trechsel, so I have to confer with my colleague, but Judge Trechsel wants you to stop there. I would like you to conclude with number 6, so I'll ask Judge Prandler what his position is. What is your decision?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: As far as I know, Judge, actually, Mr. Praljak has used at least now more than 30 minutes. We have given 20 minutes. We have more than 10 minutes used. Frankly, I don't see any major need to continue with the maps. And when our Presiding Judge said that the Chamber believes that you have understood that there are routes, that is it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. By a majority oral decision, the Chamber believes that you have used up your time. We will now just give an IC number to the references made by the witness, and we will have our break. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the latest map just marked by the witness shall be given Exhibit IC1092. Thank you, Your Honours. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Gorjanc. I'd like to thank the Judge. I wasn't granted 20 minutes. There was an agreement with Ms. Alaburic for the time that should be allocated so that I could demonstrate the frenzied fabrication of, and absurd references to, some sort of Ho Chi Min's path which served as ABiH propaganda. Throughout the time it was possible to pass through with thousands of soldiers. And nobody wants to go over there to check the roads. Your Honours, you should forget about these scholastic discussions. /unclear/ You can go to Mostar and see whether these roads can be used by cars, five or six kilometres away from HVO positions. Instead of gaining insight into basic facts, for years now we have been arguing over the banalities of whether I would get three more minutes to address the brazen lies disseminated by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, we have understood that you are very emotive about this. We will have our 20-minute break, and then we will resume with Ms. Alaburic's questions. And we will then conclude at 1900 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I give the floor to Ms. Alaburic, Judge Mindua has a question he would like to put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you. Mr. President, in fact, I do have a question I would like to put, because during the break I tried to give some thought to the various possibilities in relation to the routes, and in particular in relation to the two maps that we have had a look at, map IC1091 and IC10 -- IC1091, with regard to Kandiljan, and also the last map of Mr. Praljak's, 3D00850. So my question is as follows: Obviously, I fully understand that when one is in the eastern part of Mostar, there certainly are dozens of paths or routes, footpaths or horse paths, that can be used to move around the surroundings. I can understand that. But what I have failed to understand is the issue of the four routes, donkey routes or footpaths that we referred to immediately prior to the break. So what I would like to know is whether these paths, independent ones, that is to say, can each path be taken to leave the eastern part of Mostar and go to Jablanica or to any other place in the country, or, rather, do the four paths join up -- link up? Do the four routes lead to a main route which would be at risk of being subjected to HVO artillery fire? That's my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those four parallel routes concern a narrow stretch of eastern Mostar. It's in the area from the lower part of -- well, I can't say exactly where right now, but I know that there used to be an automobile association technical service there, and there's also a location in the northern part, the petrol station. That's where those paths, in fact, join up and form one route, and then that one route or path continues for about 500 metres, in my assessment, and then it forks off -- branches off and forms several paths that lead through Bijelo Polje. The only part that we -- the only part that is dangerous is the one that we've mentioned, the Kandiljan part. That's from the petrol station to Kandiljani, and that part of the route is just a single route which can be used by motor vehicles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Ms. Alaburic, you've asked for 40 minutes, roughly. Use your time in such a way that we can conclude with this witness today.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Good evening to everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good evening, Mr. Gorjanc. Since we're dealing with these maps and these routes, if I have understood you correctly, the Ho Chi Minh path went through Visoravni and Glogova; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, on the map that you have behind you, is Glogova shown on the map or is Glogova even further to the north, in the direction of Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Glogova Plateau isn't shown on the map, nor is the actual entrance shown or, rather, the road that forks off the main road.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Have I understood you correctly? The Ho Chi Minh path was, in fact, to the north, in the direction of Jablanica, and it can't be seen on the map?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let's return to our beautiful doctrine on All-People's Defence. Yesterday, Mr. Gorjanc, with regard to an objection raised by Judge Prandler about the All-People's Defence concept having been created in order to defend from the aggressor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Ms. Alaburic. It was not an objection which I raised, but a question. I wonder if you said objection or question, what I raised yesterday. So I raised a question, not an objection. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I didn't say "objection." I apologise if I was responsible for problems with the interpretation. I said that you initiated discussion on the matter by putting this question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And, Mr. Gorjanc, on page 29 to 31 of the transcript yesterday, you said the Yugoslav concept of All-People's Defence was created in order to defend the country from aggressors, and you said that its purpose had nothing to do with internal conflicts in Yugoslavia. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, did Yugoslavia have a military doctrine of any kind in the event of internal conflicts?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because we never assumed that something like that could happen. In 1988, there was the first law that was passed in which only military police units could be engaged. Prior to that date, this -- such engagement wasn't possible in any instructions or rules.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now show the witness certain documents?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, you have them, in fact, in front of you. Many of them are familiar to you. We've already used them. The first one is P274.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. Ms. Alaburic, do you refer, perhaps, to documents that are in the binders that are next to Mr. Stewart, because I don't know what documents you want to refer to and how I find them. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you should have been given a new set of documents. Because I didn't want you to have to consult these numerous binders, I prepared a different set.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I will look for it. Maybe I find it here. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Ms. Alaburic, do we have a new binder?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that we always prepare documents for you. If you haven't received them now, we can only give you our copy, if you need it. But these really are documents you have already seen. You could follow this by using Sanction. I know that Mr. Stringer did this. Let's have a look at P274. It's a decision on declaring a state of war. Have a look at the introductory part of the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And, Mr. Gorjanc, tell us whether the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina thought that an act of aggression had been committed against the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us how they define the aggressor?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina defines an aggressor as -- or defines the aggressor as the Republic of Serbia, the Republic of Montenegro, the Yugoslav Army, and terrorists of the Serbian Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: On the basis of this document, would you say that the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina believes that a civil war broke out in Bosnia and Herzegovina, or do they believe that an act of aggression was committed, or some other form of armed conflict had commenced?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given -- well, in view of who believes whom to be an aggressor, well, I would say that the aggression was an act of aggression committed from the outside, an external act of aggression.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Have a look at item 2. The Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina declares a state of war, and the aim is to liberate the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina from its aggressors. Does your previous answer confirm this thesis?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Have a look at item 3. It's a decision taken to organise an all-people's resistance under item 3?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, is there a significance difference between all-people's resistance and All-People's Defence?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now let's have a look at the following document, 4D1164. This is an order from the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina on stating -- on proclaiming a general public mobilisation in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Under item 1, can you tell us who is being mobilised by the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A general public mobilisation is being ordered of all military conscripts in the territory of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This includes military conscripts from the age of 18 to 55.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us whether there were any men fit for military service between 18 and 55 years of age who were not liable for military service?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there weren't.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Have a look at item 2. What does the order further state with regard to mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All citizens fit for military service, men from 18 to 65 and women from 18 to 50 -- from the years 18 to 55, are ordered to immediately report to civil protection units.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, according to these provisions, were there any men or any women fit for work who are at least 18 years of age or 55 years of age -- or 65 years of age, 55 in the case of women, were there any such individuals who were not mobilised pursuant to this decision?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Item -- under item 4, work obligation is ordered -- continuous work obligation is ordered in all public companies. Mr. Gorjanc, what are public companies? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are socially-owned companies, utility companies, electricity companies, water supply system, other companies that serve the citizens.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Have a look at item 5. Work obligation is also being ordered for all enterprises and private crafts and other shops. According to this decision, are there any people fit for work, who work in some of the companies referred to, who were not mobilised in order to perform their work obligation pursuant to this order?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no such individuals.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Have a look at item 7. It says: "A failure to adhere to this order --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation] [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, as you both speak the same language, could you make a small break, because the interpreters are crying.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I am apologising. I'm trying to follow the English interpretation. Obviously, it seems that the French booth is taking a little longer, so I'll bear that in mind. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So item 7, what would be the consequences of failure to comply with this order, Mr. Gorjanc?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Item 7 states what the consequences are of failure -- any failure to adhere to this order. Could you tell us what those consequences are?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, there's criminal responsibility and misdemeanor responsibility, or material responsibility, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's have a look at 1D942, 942. It's a platform for the activities of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina in wartime conditions. In the introductory part, it is stated that a war has been imposed by aggression on Bosnia and Herzegovina. Have a look at item 5, in which reference is made to the all-people's -- combat of all peoples, and item 6 says this is a platform which is an appeal to all citizens to join the combat against the act of aggression. Mr. Gorjanc, in your opinion, is this an example of the doctrine of All-People's Defence or is it some other kind of doctrine?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It fully corresponds to the provisions of the doctrine -- of the Yugoslav doctrine of All-People's Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. In the course of your testimony, Mr. Gorjanc, we spent a significant amount of time on defining the nature of members of armed forces and on determining the differences between definitions in accordance with international law and definitions that one finds in the Constitution of the SFRY. Amongst other things, you said, on page 46279 of the transcript, that the doctrine of All-People's Defence was not fully in accordance with international law and the protection of civilians because they don't only define members of armed forces as people who bear weapons but also citizens who aren't carrying weapons but contribute to the events of the country, such citizens are also considered as members of the armed forces. Do you remember that answer, Mr. Gorjanc?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now let's have a look at document P7. It's a manual on international law and the application of the provisions of international law. It is a voluminous document, which is why it's not contained in this set of documents. It's a document you can find in one of the Prosecution binders, but I will only refer to item 48, paragraph 3, and I think that the electronic courtroom will suffice for my purposes. In item 48, paragraph 3, there is a definition of a member of the armed forces who is not a soldier at first glance. May I assist with the page number? In the Croatian, it is page 41? Could you enlarge it a little, please? It's not paragraph 3, but paragraph 4. My mistake. It is paragraph 4. Mr. Gorjanc, could you please tell us -- it states here that a citizen, during an armed attack or in a military operation in preparation for an attack, wears no identification marks and cannot be distinguished from the civilian population, shall be considered a combatant and a member of the armed forces on condition that he openly bears arms during the military engagement and when the adversary can see him, during engagement, in military deployment which precedes the mounting of the attack. There are a few more words, but I don't think they matter. In the second paragraph, however, there is a definition of members of the armed forces of the SFRY. They are defined as members of the Yugoslav People's Army and the Territorial Defence, but also every citizen who, with arms or otherwise, takes part in resistance against attackers. Mr. Gorjanc, what we have just said from the handbook on the application of regulations of international law illustrates the difference that you have made in defining members of the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us now look at a document in my set of documents, 1D1236, 1D1236. It is the Constitution of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which in item 162, paragraph 3, says that: "Every citizen who, with arms or in another way, takes part in resisting the aggressor is a member of the armed forces of the republic." If we compare this definition with the definition from the Constitution of the SFRY, what is the conclusion we could make?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Meaning they are identical.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, in the course of your testimony, on transcript page 46311, you said, when describing the situation in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that there were three categories of prisoners of war. First, combatants; second, potential combatants or military conscripts or reserve forces; and, thirdly, other persons who, without arms, are in another way putting up resistance. Is my understanding correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: A moment ago you said, if I understood you properly, that every able-bodied man between 18 and 60 was a military conscript. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If he was subject to obligations stipulated by the regulations passed by the authorities in Sarajevo, was he a military conscript of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Gorjanc, if we recall the discussion about the isolation of Muslim soldiers in the HVO, and if we now focus on the second category of military conscripts, that is, able-bodied men of Muslim ethnicity between 16 and 60, what would you say -- to which category of war prisoners would they belong out of the three?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Able-bodied men without weapons are ranked in the second group.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: That is, potential combatants or a reserve force; is that right? The potential combatants were the reserve force; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, in answer to a question from my learned friend Ms. West and His Honour Judge Antonetti, you gave your opinion about certain situations. I would like to refer to two situations. I consider your answers to be perfectly correct. But in connection with those same facts, I will refer to a different situation. On page 46285 to 46291 - this is transcript pages - you spoke about a group of men who were at the Heliodrom. There was a four-month-old child. There were people over 80 years of age, and there were women with small children. And you said -- when asked about the arrest of these people, you said that the arrest was illegal and inhumane. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I think that your answer is quite correct, but let me ask you about a different situation. We're talking about fighting in a built-up area. The fighting has started, and as a commander of one of the two conflicting armies, you decide to launch an attack on the headquarters of the command of the enemy army. Tell me, the headquarters of the enemy command, would you consider it to be a legitimate target?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: This command is situated in a housing apartment block, and you expect the fire to be opened at the command. You assume that the command will not surrender and that the fighting could go on for at least a couple of hours. My question to you now is: It is an apartment block inhabited by thousands of people who are at risk. As a military commander, what would you do in such a situation?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would try to evacuate the population that might be at risk. Before that, I would try to warn the command about this and ask them to evacuate the population.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Would you evacuate a four-month-old baby?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, in the first place, before anyone else.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Would you evacuate a person older than 80?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Would you evacuate a woman with a small child?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, I would.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If some seven days later you were to find that the danger for them had passed, would you allow those same people to return to their homes?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My second question about a hypothetical situation refers to a question put to you by His Honour Judge Antonetti. Could you repeat the answer, Mr. Gorjanc? Seven days later, if you were to assess that the danger had passed, would you allow them to go home?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So my next question relates to your answers noted on pages 46292 up to -- I'm sorry, I misspoke. No, no, 46292 and 46296, 46296. His Honour Judge Antonetti asked you several hypothetical questions as to what you would do with inhabitants of a Muslim village, and you are an HVO commander, if you knew that your own soldiers could abuse those people and maybe even kill them. And your answer mostly was that you would have to take every possible measure to keep your soldiers under control. If you were unable to do that, to send them to the front-line; therefore, move them out of the rear, where that village is situated, et cetera. Did I understand your answer correctly?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I consider your answer a correct one. Now, let me ask you the following: You have a Muslim village in the zone of combat operations or in the immediate vicinity of that zone of combat operations. The inhabitants of those -- of that village are exposed to danger from those combat activities. Another danger threatens from several thousand Croats who were refugees or who were expelled from Central Bosnia because of ABiH activities and who are hostile towards the Muslim population in the area to which they have arrived. And as a third danger to which they are exposed are your own soldiers who have some measure of hostility towards Muslim citizens. The fighting is severe. There is a danger of losing control of the territory that you held up until then. You don't have a sufficient number of soldiers. Every single soldier is invaluable on the front-line, and you cannot spare a single soldier to guard the Muslim… inhabitants of this Muslim village. What would you do in such a situation with the Muslim inhabitants of that village or any other inhabitants of that village?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would move them outside the zone of military operations, combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Several observations about the structure of your report linked to the questions by my learned friend Ms. West. In Chapter 6, you speak about the application of the doctrine of All-People's Defence in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and in the first part of that chapter you elaborate on the regulations, the contents of the Constitution, the contents of certain regulations relating to defence, et cetera; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did the Prosecution show you a single law of Bosnia and Herzegovina or any decree relating to defence that was not contained in your report?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: With the exception of the error in the date of an amendment to the Decree on Armed Forces, did the Prosecution present any objection regarding the way in which you presented the contents of the regulations of Bosnia and Herzegovina on defence?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, asking you about this part of your report, the one relating to regulations, in a sense objected that you mentioned only four documents, and this can be found on page 46245 -- 46265, 265, and you said that you didn't quote the documents in this part of the report, but you did in another part of the report. And this answer is to be found on page 46254. So let us now look, Mr. Gorjanc, very briefly at some of the documents that you referred to in reliance to the civilian population. 4D33 -- I will list them all, and I will have a question referring to all of them. 4D33, a document of the 42nd Brigade of the 4th Corps of the ABiH, dated the 16th of April, 1993, and it says: "In villages with the Muslim nation, guard duty should be set up and full control of the village achieved." And also: "Through the bodies of the civilian authorities, achieve contact with all members of the Muslim population or require full commitment in defence of their homes." "Demand full engagement in the defence of their homes." The next document is 4D34, by the same author two days later, dated the 18th of April, and it says: "Through the bodies of the civilian authorities, achieve co-operation with the population of Dubrava and Stolac." 4D34 is the document number. The next document you quote in this part of your expert report is a document of the 42nd Mountain Brigade, dated the 18th of April. And towards the very end of the document, it says: "When drafting a plan, views and proposals should be exchanged with municipal boards and, if necessary, in agreement with other institutions of the Muslims in the territory." And at the very end of the document, it says: "Review the possibility of providing food supplies from local sources, should the need arise to use them." This document is 4D35. The next document, 4D1476, 1476, is a document of a brigade of the 3rd Corps. The date is the 31st of January, 1993, which says that: "In places of inhabitants, to secure the village, all able-bodied population should be engaged, all military conscripts, regardless of whether they are under work obligation or members of the battalion." The next document is 4D1727, 4D1727, a directive for the defence of the sovereignty and independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I will refer only to the relevant parts. In item 2, there is reference to the armed population, which needs to be united under a single command of the TO Staff. And then in item 4, there is reference to the mass resistance of citizens. In item 5, there is reference to the formation of volunteer units of the Patriotic League, patriotic forces, et cetera. Item 6.2 says that when collecting intelligence information, loyal citizens and members of the population should also be engaged. Paragraph -- item 6.4, talking about engineering security, that fortification, masking, should be carried out in co-operation with all other subjects on the territory. I could cite other passages, but we don't have enough time. And the last document in this series, 4D1603, instructions for building and strengthening combat morale of the ABiH, from February 1993, and item 1, in the first part, speaks about the unity of the army and the people and about the need to defend oneself through the assistance of the people to the army by taking care of the wounded, providing materiel, collecting information about the enemy, discovery and preventing agent provocateurs, sabotage, et cetera. And there's something else I wish to draw your attention to, sabotage activities, but we can refer to those in other documents. On the basis of all these documents and everything else that you used in your report and then that you have read, tell us, do these documents have any connection to what you described as unarmed members of the resistance?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These documents present the operationalisation of the position and doctrines of All-People's Defence in military documents, such as orders, reports, instructions, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, did my learned friend the Prosecutor show you any document emanating from the Muslim forces that would negate the application of the principles of All-People's Defence on the part of the BiH Army?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, you have dedicated a whole chapter to the doctrine of All-People's Defence in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and you speak about sabotage actions. Are they part of the doctrine of All-People's Defence?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to be very precise in the interpretation of the term "sabotage." This refers to the activities behind the enemy lines with infiltrated forces or the forces that have been there from before and are armed. These are not classical sabotage actions.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's look at two general documents to see whether sabotage actions were part and form of struggle on the part of the BiH Army. The first document is 4D1730. This is an analysis of combat activities undertaken by the 3rd Corps, and the document was issued in February 1993. In the very introduction, a reference is made to the All-People's Defence or resistance put up against the aggressor. And in the last part of the second paragraph, it says that most of the intelligence was collected through units in contact through observation or by gathering intelligence from the population. Tell me, please, the claim about the intelligence co-operation with the population, is that part of unarmed resistance put up against the aggressor?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In bullet point 14, it says: "Continue an even bigger application of the infiltration of sabotage groups behind the enemy lines and tell them to carry out sabotage activities." Judging by this document, what would you say, Mr. Gorjanc? Were sabotage actions an important part of the activities of the BiH Army?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In every respect, because sabotage action behind enemy lines brings much more results than operations on the front-line and engages fewer men.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And now let's look at 4D1240, 1240. This is a directive by the Staff of the Supreme Command of the Armed Forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina, dated September 1992, and let's look at bullet point number 4, where reference is made to the forces which should be engaged in lifting the blockade of Sarajevo and engaged in the defence of free territory and offensive, whereas auxiliary forces have to be used for sabotage actions behind enemy lines. Mr. Gorjanc, do tell us, were there any special units that were engaged in sabotage activities or should there be any -- some other interpretation of these words?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, in the BiH Army there were no special units, but some more courageous soldiers would infiltrate themselves behind the enemy lines, or there were some special-purpose units, such as the 7th, the Black Swans, and Mujahedin, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In Chapter 6 of this document, there is a list of all the contents of an armed struggle, and the last is: "Sabotage and anti-sabotage struggle." And it says here: "Carry out large-scale sabotage activities behind the enemy lines and prevent them from bringing in fresh troops and fresh supplies, and thus inflicting as much damage as possible." Judging by this document, Mr. Gorjanc, what would you say about sabotage activities as a form of struggle undertaken by the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that this was a very important element and form of combat activities for the BiH Army, given the fact that they always and constantly emphasised that problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In Chapter 7, about intelligence support, it says: "The tasks of intelligence support should involve intelligence bodies, surveillance units, and the population." Would you say that this is also one form of non-armed resistance put up against the aggressors?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we please go into private session -- into closed session?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to mention just a few witnesses who testified in this courtroom and said that they were familiar with the existence of the corridor and the possibility for people to leave Mostar: Mr. Kemal Lizde, in P10137, paragraph 26; Witness DW, transcript 23261; Witness BB, to Ms. Nozica's question, transcript 9851.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gorjanc, I will have some questions about what Mr. Cedric Thornberry told us here in this courtroom. Do you know who that was?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Who was he?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was one of the negotiators in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: He was also a member of UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In any case --

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's how I know him.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: On page 26266 and 26267, told us that he was aware of the corridor, and then he went on to tell us that in the month of August and early September 1993, a media campaign was organised which was supposed to reveal for the whole world what the situation in East Mostar was. He said, literally, that the campaign was directed at the population of western states and that it was expected that they would put pressure on the governments of their respective countries in order to undertake more energetic measures in order to resolve problems in Mostar. This was recorded on page 26274. Mr. Gorjanc, as a person who worked in the Centre for Strategic Studies in Slovenia, could you please tell us something about media campaigns that were organised by the BiH Army or Alija Izetbegovic's government?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of such campaigns was the siege of Sarajevo. It is my deep belief that if they had wanted to call -- to talk before that, they would have reached an agreement, especially in view of the fact that Karadzic publicly appealed to them at this Assembly session not to organise the referendum. Further on, such a campaign was showing victims. I read some memoirs, for example the one written by General McKenzie, who wrote about the shell that landed in Sarajevo, and similar things. There was many such things, not only in Bosnia. It was -- it started also already in Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And just one more question because we're coming up to 7.00. Mr. Gorjanc, if somebody were to show you a document that would demonstrate that Alija Izetbegovic's government deliberately pursued a policy to present themselves as a victim, would that fit into what you have just told us about media campaigns?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GORJANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. It seems to me that one such document does exist. Its author is Halilovic, who says in it that, We should stop being a victim and that we should start relying on our own powers and strengths.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This brings my additional examination to the end. Thank you very much, Mr. Gorjanc, for having come here to testify on behalf of Mr. Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, on behalf of my colleagues I would like to thank you for having come here and testifying for almost two weeks. I wish you a safe journey back to your country. As everybody knows, we have a witness only next week. I looked at the distribution of time this morning. I hope that the witness will be at the disposal of the Chamber on Monday at 2.15. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
